sections.title: 30. Turn the journey into your own English
paragraphs: You do not need to learn every technical word before enjoying the story. Read a few sections, choose five useful words, and say something with them immediately. For example: “The island has steep cliffs.” Then add a reason or contrast: “The rock is ancient, but its present shape developed later.”

For a first session, read the arrival, names and map chapters, then describe the location for 45 seconds. In a second session, read the geology chapters and explain the formation process using first, then, gradually and eventually. In a third session, read the film, community and conservation chapters and give your opinion about responsible tourism.

The Words section contains English definitions, Armenian translations and contextual examples. Practice includes comprehension questions, missing-word exercises and two grammar lessons. Speak offers tasks with suggested language and a way to check your own answer. Use the website's listening controls where your browser provides a suitable voice, then read a short paragraph aloud yourself.

Finish with this challenge: imagine a friend has just asked, “Is James Bond Island only a rock?” Answer for one minute without reading the article. Include its real names, one fact about its formation, the film connection, and one reason the wider bay matters. Your goal is a clear explanation in your own words, not a perfect performance from memory.

quiz.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes Khao Phing Kan from Ko Tapu?
options: Khao Phing Kan is the larger island site; Ko Tapu is the narrow offshore pillar.
Khao Phing Kan is the narrow pillar; Ko Tapu is the larger island site.
Khao Phing Kan is a village on stilts; Ko Tapu is the name of the entire bay.
Khao Phing Kan and Ko Tapu are two names for Phuket’s main airport.
quiz.explanation: The popular name James Bond Island can blur two features. Visitors explore the larger Khao Phing Kan site and look toward the separate limestone pillar, Ko Tapu.

quiz.question: Which film and cast correctly explain the site’s James Bond connection?
options: Dr. No (1962): Sean Connery as Bond and Joseph Wiseman as the main villain.
Goldfinger (1964): Sean Connery as Bond and Gert Fröbe as the main villain.
The Man with the Golden Gun (1974): Roger Moore as Bond and Christopher Lee as Scaramanga.
Casino Royale (2006): Daniel Craig as Bond and Mads Mikkelsen as the main villain.
quiz.explanation: The relevant film is The Man with the Golden Gun, released in 1974. Roger Moore played James Bond and Christopher Lee played Francisco Scaramanga. The other options name different Bond films.

quiz.question: Which explanation best describes the origin of the limestone discussed in the story?
options: It began as molten lava that cooled into the pillar’s modern shape.
Carbonate-rich material accumulated in ancient seas and eventually became rock.
Builders piled blocks around a metal support for the film production.
A single storm compressed beach sand into solid rock within a few hours.
quiz.explanation: The story separates the formation of limestone from the much later shaping of the landscape. Carbonate sediments can accumulate, become buried and harden into limestone over geological time.

quiz.question: Why is slightly acidic water important in the development of limestone karst?
options: It immediately melts limestone into liquid rock.
It prevents any change from taking place inside cracks.
It turns limestone directly into mangrove roots.
It can dissolve limestone and gradually enlarge cracks and passages.
quiz.explanation: Weakly acidic water can react with the calcium carbonate in limestone. Over long periods, this dissolution helps enlarge cracks, caves and other karst features.

quiz.question: Why should we distinguish the age of the rock from the age of the present landscape?
options: A rock becomes younger every time a visitor photographs it.
The film company replaced the ancient rock with a new copy in 1974.
Ancient rock can be uplifted, dissolved and eroded into younger landforms.
The age of a rock is always exactly the same as the age of its current shoreline.
quiz.explanation: Rock formation and landscape development are different stages. Old limestone can later be raised, cracked, weathered, eroded and surrounded by changing sea levels.

quiz.question: Two photographs taken several hours apart show different amounts of exposed rock at the waterline. Which process can explain this?
options: The tide has raised or lowered the water level.
The entire pillar has grown several metres in a few hours.
The limestone has changed into a different type of rock.
The island has moved from one province to another.
quiz.explanation: Tides change water levels during the day, exposing or covering parts of the shoreline. Such a short-term difference does not mean the whole rock has changed shape.

quiz.question: Why do mangroves matter to the bay’s living environment?
options: They exist only to hide buildings from tourist photographs.
They remove the need to protect other habitats in the bay.
They guarantee that every boat trip will have calm weather.
Their roots and surrounding habitat provide shelter for living things.
quiz.explanation: Mangroves are functioning habitats. Their roots and sheltered waters offer protection and support life; their value goes well beyond their appearance in a photograph.

quiz.question: Which description avoids confusing the identities of communities in the region?
options: Everyone who lives near the sea belongs to the same cultural community.
Ko Panyi is a Thai Muslim community and should not automatically be identified as Moken.
Ko Panyi’s residents are actors who live permanently inside a film set.
The names Ko Panyi and Ko Tapu refer to the same residential village.
quiz.explanation: Living by the sea does not make different communities interchangeable. Ko Panyi is a separate Thai Muslim village; Moken communities have their own identities and histories.

quiz.question: What is the appropriate way to enjoy the view of Ko Tapu?
options: Use permitted viewpoints and follow current park instructions about distance and access.
Ask the boat driver to ignore barriers for a closer photograph.
Climb the pillar whenever another visitor appears to be doing so.
Break off a small piece of limestone as evidence of the visit.
quiz.explanation: The lesson treats conservation rules as part of the visit. Viewing the pillar from permitted places protects the site and respects the people responsible for managing it.

quiz.question: Which visitor best applies the story’s approach to informed, respectful tourism?
options: A visitor who treats every house as a public attraction.
A visitor who assumes a film tells the full history of a real community.
A visitor who learns the place names, follows guidance and asks before photographing residents.
A visitor who judges the whole bay only by whether one photograph matches a poster.
quiz.explanation: Understanding the place includes its geology, names and living communities. Respecting guidance and people’s privacy makes the visit more considerate as well as more meaningful.

speaking.prompt: 45 seconds — Open the photograph of Ko Tapu. Describe what you can actually see: its shape, the water, the surrounding islands and one detail of the rock. Finish with one question you would like to ask a guide.
speaking.tip: Start: “In the centre, I can see …” Continue: “Its base looks …” and “In the background …” Use pillar, silhouette and limestone. Self-check: Did you describe at least three visible details? Did you separate what you see from what you only guess?

speaking.prompt: 60 seconds — A friend says, “I thought James Bond Island was just one rock!” Explain the difference between Khao Phing Kan, Ko Tapu and the wider Phang Nga Bay. Use the lesson’s map or photographs as a guide.
speaking.tip: Build your answer with “The larger site is …”, “The pillar beside it is …” and “Both are in …”. End: “So when a tour uses the name James Bond Island, ask …”. Self-check: Did you use the three names correctly and explain one possible misunderstanding?

speaking.prompt: 90 seconds — Explain to a curious teenager how an ancient seabed can eventually become a landscape of limestone islands. Describe the main stages and explain why the age of the rock is not the age of the modern pillar’s shape.
speaking.tip: Use “First …”, “Over time …”, “Later …” and “Finally …”. Include sediment, uplift, dissolve and erosion. Try two passive sentences, such as “Sediment was deposited …”. Self-check: Did you distinguish rock formation from later shaping? Did you avoid saying that one storm or one volcano created the whole landscape?

speaking.prompt: 90 seconds — Tell a friend why a real place can become famous through a fictional story. Explain the 1974 James Bond connection, then discuss one benefit and one possible difficulty that film fame can bring to a destination.
speaking.tip: For history use past simple: “The film was released …”. For an ongoing connection use present perfect: “The place has become …”. Add “One benefit could be …” and “One challenge could be …”. Self-check: Did you name the correct film? Did you label possible impacts as your reasoning rather than inventing visitor statistics?

speaking.prompt: 2 minutes — Role-play a conversation with a tour operator. You want to see James Bond Island, learn about the bay and visit any included caves responsibly. Ask five useful questions, then explain which answers would help you choose an excursion.
speaking.tip: Ask: “Which pier do we leave from?”, “Is the park fee included?”, “How does the tide affect the itinerary?”, “Who decides whether a cave is safe to enter?” and “How much time do we have at each stop?”. Add your own question about group size or local guidance. Self-check: Did you use polite questions and clarify what is included without assuming a price or promising access?

speaking.prompt: 2 minutes — Imagine you are helping design a better visitor experience for Phang Nga Bay. Propose three practical choices that protect nature, respect residents and support local livelihoods. Explain one trade-off and finish with the choice you consider most important.
speaking.tip: Use “I would suggest … because …”, “This could help …”, “However, we would need to consider …” and “My priority would be …”. Include conservation, livelihood, sustainable and perspective. Self-check: Did each proposal have a reason? Did you consider residents as people with their own needs rather than as part of the scenery?

grammar.title: Passive voice: explain what happens to a place
grammar.explanation: Use the passive when the action or the thing affected is more important than the person doing it. Form: subject + be + past participle. In the present simple, use is or are: “The coastline is shaped by water.” In the past simple, use was or were: “The film was released in 1974.” Use by when the agent or cause is useful; omit it when it is unknown, obvious or unimportant. Compare “Rainwater dissolves limestone” with “Limestone is dissolved by rainwater.” Both describe the same process, but the passive puts limestone first. Armenian guide: կրավորական սեռը շեշտում է, թե ինչ է կատարվում առարկայի հետ։ “The film was released”՝ «Ֆիլմը թողարկվել է»։ A passive sentence still needs the correct tense. Do not omit be: write “The rock is shaped”, not “The rock shaped”, when you mean that a process acts on the rock. Also distinguish a process from a result: a crack may be widened by water over time; this does not mean all cracks have the same origin.
examples: Present passive: “Limestone is slowly dissolved by slightly acidic water.”
Past passive: “Sediment was deposited on an ancient seabed.”
Past passive without an agent: “The Man with the Golden Gun was released in 1974.”
Active → passive: “Water enlarges some cracks.” → “Some cracks are enlarged by water.”
grammar.exercise: Rewrite these sentences in the passive, keeping their original tense. 1) Water shapes the coastline. 2) The studio released the film in 1974. 3) Visitors photograph the pillar. Then explain why the agent can be omitted in sentence 2.
grammar.answer: 1) The coastline is shaped by water. 2) The film was released in 1974 (by the studio). 3) The pillar is photographed by visitors. In sentence 2, the film and its release date are the focus, so naming the studio is unnecessary unless that information matters to the discussion.

grammar.title: Past simple or present perfect: a finished event or a link to now?
grammar.explanation: Use the past simple for a completed event at a finished past time: “The film came out in 1974.” Time expressions such as yesterday, last year and in 1974 usually point to this form. Use the present perfect, have or has + past participle, for experience up to now or a past development with a present connection: “Have you ever visited Phang Nga Bay?” and “The film has made the location familiar to many viewers.” The second sentence focuses on a result that matters now, without specifying a finished time. Since names the starting point; for names a duration. A connection can continue: “The site has been associated with James Bond since 1974.” Armenian guide: Past simple-ը պատմում է ավարտված անցյալի իրադարձության մասին, իսկ present perfect-ը անցյալը կապում է ներկայի հետ։ Հայերեն թարգմանության ձևը միշտ չէ, որ միանշանակ ցույց է տալիս անգլերենի ճիշտ ժամանակաձևը։ Ask yourself: Am I saying when a completed event happened, or am I discussing experience or a result up to now? Do not combine a present-perfect event with a finished time: say “I visited the island yesterday”, not “I have visited the island yesterday”.
examples: Finished event: “Roger Moore played Bond in The Man with the Golden Gun.”
Finished time: “The film was released in 1974.”
Experience up to now: “Have you ever seen a limestone sea stack?”
Continuing connection: “The site has been associated with James Bond since 1974.”
Model travel conversation: “Have you visited the bay?” — “Yes, I visited it last year.” The question asks about experience; the answer gives a finished time.
grammar.exercise: Choose the correct form. 1) The film (was released / has been released) in 1974. 2) (Did you ever see / Have you ever seen) a sea stack? I mean at any time in your life up to now. 3) Model diary sentence: We (visited / have visited) Khao Phing Kan yesterday. 4) The site (was / has been) associated with James Bond since 1974. Finally, correct this model learner sentence: “I have learned the two place names yesterday.”
grammar.answer: 1) was released — 1974 is a finished past time. 2) Have you ever seen — the question covers experience up to now. 3) visited — yesterday is a finished time. 4) has been — since 1974 marks a connection continuing to the present. Correction: “I learned the two place names yesterday.” Without a finished time, “I have learned the two place names” can emphasise what I now know.
